"Vishal fell asleep in the lab again," Usha said, dropping a tray on the canteen table. "Third time this week."
"Maybe he's tired," said Paromita.
"Tired from what? Scrolling all night? He's just lazy. Our circuit report is due Friday and he's done one graph."
"Did you ask him?"
"Why should I? It's obvious."
Paromita stirred her tea. "He leaves the hostel at ten every night. I've seen him."
"Exactly. Partying."
"In a delivery jacket?"
Usha paused. "What?"
"A delivery company jacket. He comes back at five. His dad's shop shut last year, I think."
Usha looked down at the plate. "He never said anything."
"Would you, if everyone had already decided you were lazy?"

passage: Last semester, in our supply chain group, I was the one who called Manoj lazy, loudly, in the group chat. He'd missed two meetings and his slides came in at 2 am, full of typos. I wrote, "Some of us actually care about grades." I'm Dhruv, and I've replayed that line a lot since. What I didn't know was that Manoj worked the night shift at a call centre near the station, eleven to six, to pay his sister's school fees. He saw my message and never argued back. I learned the truth from a senior who worked there too. Looking back, there were so many clues: the red eyes, the office lanyard in his bag, the way he always ate breakfast at noon. I just read every clue as proof of his character.

Mentor's note, Year 2 design project, Group C
During today's review, Suraj told me Wasim "does nothing and should get a lower grade." Wasim had missed both lab slots this week, and the prototype casing was unfinished. Suraj seemed genuinely angry, arms crossed, and said, "He just doesn't bother."
I spoke with Wasim separately. He has a night job at a bakery, to support his family, and had been nodding off at the lathe. He had not told the group, out of embarrassment.
With Wasim's permission, I told Suraj only that Wasim has a work commitment in the evenings. Suraj was quiet, then asked if the group could move its lab slot to mornings. We agreed on Tuesday and Thursday, 9 am.
Follow-up in two weeks.
Dr Rekha Menon

You asked about our group project in second year? Okay. I'm Pema, and I owe Yusuf an apology I only made later.

There were four of us. Yusuf kept missing the evening meetings. When he did come, he looked half asleep. I told the others, "He's just lazy. Always has been." I was annoyed every time I saw his name in the chat.

Then one night I went to buy tea near the railway station at eleven, and I saw Yusuf behind the counter of a twenty-four-hour pharmacy, in a uniform, stacking boxes.

He saw me and looked embarrassed. Later he told me he'd been working night shifts since his father's shop closed. He attended college in the day and worked till two.

Week one. Zeenat was assigned to a lab group with Tushar. He arrived late to the first session, yawning. She thought, great, a lazy one.

Week three. Tushar missed a deadline for his part of the report. Zeenat complained to the others. "He's just careless. I'm doing his part." She didn't ask him why.

Week five. Zeenat went to the canteen early, before seven, and saw Tushar coming out of the kitchen in an apron, carrying crates. The canteen manager said, "He's been working the night-to-morning shift here since his mother lost her job."

Zeenat felt her stomach drop. She'd been sure it was his character. It had never crossed her mind that something invisible was pressing on him.

That afternoon she found him in the library. "I'm sorry. I didn't know. Can we split the report differently so it works with your shifts?"

He looked relieved. "Thank you. I didn't know how to say it."

qa.a: Carrying crates.

qa.a: Zeenat felt her stomach drop, ashamed that she had blamed his character without imagining hidden pressures.

qa.a: Zeenat apologised and offered to split the report around his shifts, which dealt with the real problem instead of blaming.

qa.a: Tushar looked relieved, saying he hadn't known how to tell anyone.

Anand, you said your roommate is lazy because he sleeps all afternoon? Hmm. Sit. Your Indu aunty has a story.

When I was nineteen, at college in Madurai, our group had a boy called Selvam. He always came late to morning lectures. He fell asleep in the library. I said to everyone, "Selvam is lazy. Don't give him anything important."

One night, going home late from a wedding, I passed the bus depot. There was Selvam, washing buses under a street light. At one in the morning.

I found out later he washed buses every night to pay his hostel fees. His family were farmers, and it had been a bad year.

I felt so ashamed. I'd judged him by the sleepy face I saw, never thinking about the nights I didn't see.

So, Anand, have you asked your roommate what his nights are like?

qa.a: Selvam probably felt tired and hurt, carrying a heavy load no one knew about.
